setupSteps: Mat and space. Lay the mat on a flat, non-slip floor with about 1.8 m clear, away from the wall and furniture; or place a sturdy chair on a non-slip floor (no wheels).
Clothes. Loose pants or leggings with some stretch; avoid very tight jeans that block the hip bend. Tuck in a long kurta so it does not bunch under the hips. Remove shoes for the lying version.
Props ready. Thin pillow or folded towel under the head if the chin lifts; strap, belt or dupatta (long enough to loop behind the thigh); wall space for the foot-on-wall version.

Starting position (lying). Lie on the back with both knees bent, feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, arms resting by the sides. Keep the low back resting on the floor in its natural curve (not pressed flat, not arched hard).
Starting position (chair). Sit near the front of the chair with both feet flat on the floor, knees at about 90 degrees (est.), spine tall.
Camera. Phone on a low stool at mat height, 2 m to the side of the mat at hip level, landscape, so the head, shoulders, hips, knees and ankles are in frame (see section 11).

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Lie down and set the feet
steps.action: lie on your back, knees bent, both feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
steps.feel: back resting on the floor, neck relaxed.
steps.visualCheck: side view, knees up, back flat on the mat; front view, knees level.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Pick the side and lift the foot
steps.action: lift the right foot off the floor.
steps.feel: weight stays even through the shoulders and left foot.
steps.visualCheck: only one foot on the floor, hips level.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Cross the ankle over the knee
steps.action: rest the right ankle across the left thigh, just above the left knee (on the thigh, not on the kneecap), and let the right knee fall gently out to the side so the legs make a "4".
steps.feel: a light stretch in the right buttock already; no pinch in the right knee or hip.
steps.visualCheck: front view, a clear "4" shape; the right foot flexed (toes pulled toward the shin) to protect the knee.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Flex the crossed foot
steps.action: gently flex the right foot, pulling the toes toward the shin, and keep it that way.
steps.feel: the ankle and knee feel stable.
steps.visualCheck: foot not floppy or pointing, ankle in line with the shin.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Stay here or draw the thigh closer
steps.action: this is already a stretch for many people. To feel more, slide the left foot a little farther from the hips; to feel less, slide it closer (Hinge Health suggests the heel closer to the buttocks for an easier version). Simplest for beginners: leave the left foot on the floor and just stop here.
steps.visualCheck: the right knee stays open, not collapsing in.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Optional deeper level: lift the supporting foot
steps.action: only if step 5 feels easy, lift the left foot off the floor so the left shin is parallel to the floor (knee above hip, about 90 degrees, est.).
steps.feel: a deeper stretch deep in the right buttock; the low back stays on the floor.
steps.visualCheck: side view, left shin roughly level with the floor, low back still down.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Optional deeper level: hold behind the thigh
steps.action: thread the right hand through the gap and the left hand around the outside, and clasp the hands behind the left thigh (or loop a strap behind the thigh). Draw the left thigh gently toward the chest.
steps.feel: a deepening stretch in the right buttock, never a sharp pull in the hip or knee.
steps.breathing: breathe out as you draw in.
steps.visualCheck: head and shoulders stay down on the mat; neck long.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Hold and breathe
steps.action: stay still, press the tailbone gently toward the floor, and breathe slowly.
steps.feel: light effort 3-4/10 on the ACSM 0-10 effort scale (= Borg 9-11 on the 6-20 scale); a firm stretch, never pain, no tingling or numbness down the leg.
steps.breathing: slow breaths in through the nose, long out through the mouth, 3-5 breaths.
steps.visualCheck: body still, shoulders and head resting, ribs moving slightly.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Release
steps.action: let go of the thigh, set the left foot back on the floor, and lift the right foot off the knee. Hug both knees for one breath.
steps.visualCheck: legs come down smoothly, no jerk.

steps.part: A. Supine figure-4 with the foot on the floor (the beginner default)
steps.title: Repeat on the other side
steps.feel: compare the sides; one is often tighter.

steps.title: Sit tall near the front of the chair. Feet flat, spine long, shoulders relaxed, both hips on the seat. Breath normal

Cross the ankle over the knee. Lift the right ankle and rest it across the left thigh just above the knee. Let the right knee open out. Flex the right foot. Visual check: side view, torso upright; front view, both hips level on the seat

Hinge forward. Keep the back long and lean forward from the hips (not the waist) until a stretch is felt in the right buttock. Do not hunch the shoulders. You can rest the hands on the crossed shin or on the thighs. Breath out as you lean

Hold 20-30 seconds (est.) breathing slowly, then sit up slowly and switch sides. Cleveland Clinic and desk-wellness sources support the same sit-and-lean form. If the crossed knee sits high above the other, put a folded towel or book under the planted foot or use a lower footstool so the pelvis stays level (est.)
Hip-replacement and similar warnings apply: leaning forward while sitting takes the hip beyond 90 degrees and crossing the legs is on the usual posterior-approach "avoid" list (section 9)

commonMistakes.title: Pressing the crossed knee away with the hand
commonMistakes.text: Pressing the crossed knee away with the hand. It forces rotation through the knee, not the hip. Fix: keep the hand behind the supporting thigh, let the crossed knee open by itself, and keep the foot flexed (Cleveland Clinic warns against yanking; the Hinge Health guide uses a gentle pull).

commonMistakes.title: Letting the ankle rest on the kneecap
commonMistakes.text: Letting the ankle rest on the kneecap. It pinches the knee. Fix: place the ankle across the lower thigh just above the knee.

commonMistakes.title: Pointing the crossed foot
commonMistakes.text: Pointing the crossed foot. It lets the ankle roll and loads the outside of the knee. Fix: flex the foot (toes toward the shin).

commonMistakes.title: Twisting the low back to get closer
commonMistakes.text: Twisting the low back to get closer. It adds spinal load, and a handout advises against letting the back twist (a PT-style handout, via search result). Fix: keep the pelvis level; reduce the range instead.

commonMistakes.title: Lifting the head and shoulders off the floor and cranking the neck
commonMistakes.text: Lifting the head and shoulders off the floor and cranking the neck. Neck strain. Fix: rest the head down or use a thin pillow; use a strap if you cannot reach.

commonMistakes.title: Pulling hard, bouncing or holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Pulling hard, bouncing or holding the breath. Raises the risk of a muscle or joint strain and tension. Fix: stay at a "mild tightness" level, hold still, and breathe out slowly (ACSM guidance is stretch to mild tightness or slight discomfort).

commonMistakes.title: Pushing through tingling, numbness or sharp pain down the leg
commonMistakes.text: Pushing through tingling, numbness or sharp pain down the leg. That can mean the sciatic nerve is being irritated or compressed, not just muscles stretching. Fix: ease off, change position, and stop if it does not settle immediately (Cleveland Clinic and Spine-health on sciatic symptoms).

commonMistakes.title: Seated: hunching and twisting instead of hinging
commonMistakes.text: Seated: hunching and twisting instead of hinging. Strains the spine and gives a weak glute stretch. Fix: sit tall and lean from the hips with a flat back.

commonMistakes.title: Doing it with a hip replacement without clearance
commonMistakes.text: Doing it with a hip replacement without clearance. The shape crosses the legs and bends the hip past 90 degrees, which posterior-approach precautions forbid. Fix: ask the surgeon or physio first (section 9).

safetyNotes: Knees (crossed leg): the crossed ankle sits on the knee or thigh and the knee is opened outward, which can twist the knee if forced. Keep the foot flexed, rest the ankle on the thigh not the kneecap, never press the knee, and stop for sharp or catching pain. Sucirandhrasana teaching lists knee injury as a contraindication (Pranayoga). A stretch-therapist source says stretches can irritate the meniscus and ligaments when flexibility is limited or the joint is unstable, so use a gentle controlled range (Fit&Well). For knee pain use the foot-on-floor or chair version, or skip it.

Hip flexion limits: the pose bends the hip of the supporting leg toward the chest and the crossed hip outward. After a total hip replacement (posterior approach), standard precautions say do not flex the hip past 90 degrees, do not cross the legs at the knees or ankles, and avoid turning the hip inward (a clinical guideline table and a physio source; West Suffolk NHS leaflet exists but its text could not be read here). A 2019 Hospital for Special Surgery study and a 2020 systematic review of 7 studies found no effect on dislocation rates from following hip precautions in posterior-approach replacements, but your surgeon's own instructions take priority. Do NOT use the figure-4 (lying or seated) unless your surgeon or physio clears it. Hip pain with a pinching "catch" in the front of the hip is another reason to ease off (hip impingement is a known issue with deep hip flexion; clinical source for this pose Not found).

Sciatic symptoms and piriformis syndrome: stretching is a common part of conservative care, but buttock pain is not always piriformis syndrome. Stop if the stretch increases leg pain, tingling or numbness. See a doctor promptly for loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around the groin or inner thighs (saddle area), new or worsening leg weakness, severe pain after a fall or injury, or fever with back pain (Spine-health red-flag list, Cleveland Clinic).
Lower back: the lying version with the low back resting is gentle for most people, but do not twist the back to get closer; stop if back pain or leg symptoms increase.
Sacroiliac (SI) joint pain: Sucirandhrasana teaching lists sacroiliac issues as a contraindication (Pranayoga); a clinical source for the figure-4 specifically is Not found. Reduce range or skip.

Osteoporosis: use the gentle, foot-on-floor version; do not force the knee or pull with the arms or twist the spine (UK consensus statement on osteoporosis exercise; IOF). Ask a doctor with a known fracture.

Pregnancy: after about 16 weeks, avoid lying flat on the back for long periods (Tommy's). Choose the seated chair version with an upright torso and no deep fold over the belly; one article notes that people told not to lie flat may prefer seated or standing figure-4s. Check with the midwife or doctor.
Balance: standing figure-4 is a single-leg stretch and not for beginners with balance concerns; stay with lying or seated versions.
Recent surgery (hip, knee, spine, abdomen): wait for the surgeon or physio before crossing the legs or drawing the thigh to the chest.

Stop immediately if you feel: sharp or catching pain in the hip, groin or knee; tingling, burning or numbness down the leg; pain that spreads or gets worse after releasing; dizziness; or in pregnancy any pressure or pain in the belly.

Gym etiquette: use the stretching area or a mat out of walkways; wipe the mat after use; do not lie in a walkway. At the office, keep the chair stable and non-rolling; do not do it on a wheeled chair.

Hold time: 15-30 s (handouts) vs 30-60 s (desk and general sources); ACSM 10-30 s for most adults, 30-60 s for older adults. We chose 20-30 s per side, 2 rounds.
Seated vs lying: lying gives a stronger, more controlled stretch; seated is easier and works at the desk and in pregnancy but is milder. We offer both, with lying as the default.
Which muscle: called piriformis, glute or hip-rotator stretch depending on the source; we describe the whole buttock and deep rotator group.

Benefit strength: the figure-4 is widely used in piriformis and sciatic-type programmes, but evidence is mostly small studies and clinical guidance; one small trial found no extra immediate rotation gain after a warm-up. We list comfort and flexibility, not cure claims.

Hip-replacement precautions: guideline tables say no flexion past 90 degrees and no leg crossing after posterior-approach replacement; a 2019 HSS study and a 2020 systematic review found no dislocation difference without precautions. We chose "ask a doctor" and the surgeon's own rules win.
Sucirandhrasana vs figure-4: same lying leg shape; some teachers add a rotation of the legs to the side. We treat the rotation as an advanced option.
Official AYUSH step text: Not found (Sucirandhrasana does not appear in the CYP list as far as secondary summaries show).
